concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: German uses the Latin alphabet, and thousands of everyday words came into German and English from Latin — directly, and through French — Nation, Information, Restaurant, Kaffee. You can already recognize them before you speak a word of German. The words below are the first ones to say out loud: hallo opens almost every conversation, danke answers kindness, ja and nein steer it.
concepts.commonError: Say hallo the moment you arrive — Germans notice silence more than accent. Save tschüss (goodbye) for leaving.

concepts.title: Introducing yourself
concepts.explanation: Ich heiße introduces your name: Ich heiße Anna. Ich bin means I am and can also introduce you: Ich bin Anna. Ask a peer Wie heißt du? Notice the ending: ich heiße, but du heißt. Freut mich is a short way to say nice to meet you. Keep ich when you write these complete statements.
concepts.commonError: Use heiße with ich and heißt with du. Keep the capital letter at the beginning of a sentence.

concepts.title: Polite café requests
concepts.explanation: Ich möchte means I would like. Learn einen Kaffee and einen Tee as complete request chunks: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. Kaffee and Tee are masculine nouns. Here they are the requested objects, so the article is einen. You will explore that pattern later; for now, swap the drink and keep einen. Bitte adds please; danke expresses thanks.

examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.
I would like a tea, please.

concepts.commonError: Use einen in these requests, not ein. German nouns keep their capitals: Kaffee and Tee.

concepts.title: Numbers and quantities
concepts.explanation: German numbers are useful as short runs before you calculate with them. Learn one through ten, then use Was kostet? to ask the price of one thing. One apple is ein Apfel; two apples are zwei Äpfel. Keep each noun's capital letter.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Use ein with one masculine Apfel and zwei with plural Äpfel. German nouns are capitalized.

description: Four A1 German lessons: first words, introductions, polite café requests, and numbers for everyday quantities. Native-speaker editorial review remains open.

lessons.title: First words
lessons.objective: Recognize and say your first German words — greetings and Latin-shared words — before building any sentences.
lessons.explanation: You already know hundreds of German words: Nation, Information, Restaurant. They came into English and German from Latin, the common root of the Romance languages — French, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese — which is why German shares so many recognizable words with them. Today you only say a few out loud: hallo, danke, ja, nein. No sentences yet — those come next.
lessons.culturalNote: German capitalizes every noun — Nation, Kaffee. The capital letter is part of the spelling.

exercises.prompt: You already know this word — it opens almost every conversation in Germany. «Hallo» — what does it mean?
exercises.explanation: Hallo. is hello — the first word to say out loud. The rest of this lesson stays this small.

exercises.prompt: Think: you walk into a bakery in Berlin. One word greets the baker before anything else. Say it in your head — then write it.
exercises.explanation: Hallo. One word, said first, opens the conversation.

exercises.prompt: Nation, Information, Restaurant — spelled almost the same in English and German. Why do you already recognize them?
answers: German and English share thousands of words from Latin.
options: German and English share thousands of words from Latin.
German borrowed its everyday words from modern English.
exercises.explanation: Both languages inherited these words from Latin — the common root of the Romance languages. Recognition comes before production.

exercises.prompt: Give the English meaning: Danke.
exercises.explanation: Danke is thank you — the second word to say out loud.

exercises.prompt: Complete the first word you say when you arrive: ___
exercises.explanation: Hallo. — said before everything else.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange. How many times do you read the word for thank you?
exercises.passage: — Hallo ! — Hallo. — Danke ? — Ja, danke. — Nein, danke.
exercises.explanation: Every word on this page is one you already learned.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the model: first words.
exercises.explanation: Two words you can say. Replay slowly, then at normal speed.

lessons.title: Introducing yourself
lessons.objective: Introduce yourself, ask a name, and respond to an introduction.
lessons.explanation: Ich heiße introduces your name: Ich heiße Anna. Ich bin means I am and can also introduce you: Ich bin Anna. Ask a peer Wie heißt du? Notice the ending: ich heiße, but du heißt. Freut mich is a short way to say nice to meet you. Keep ich when you write these complete statements.
lessons.culturalNote: Wie heißt du? uses informal du for peers. German has a separate formal form with Sie; this lesson practices only the informal question.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase asks another person their name in German?
exercises.explanation: Use the complete name question when meeting someone.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to introduce Anna by name.
exercises.explanation: Use heiße with ich and heißt with du. Keep the capital letter at the beginning of a sentence.

exercises.prompt: Read the first meeting. Who gives their own name?
exercises.explanation: The person who uses the name phrase introduces themself.
exercises.passage:
Anna: Hallo. Ich heiße Anna.
Leo: Hallo. Freut mich.
exercises.translation:
Anna: Hello. My name is Anna.
Leo: Hello. Nice to meet you.

exercises.prompt: Say “Nice to meet you” using the short expression taught here.
exercises.explanation: Use this short response after an introduction.

exercises.prompt: Imagine meeting a new classmate. Introduce yourself as Anna, using the phrase that means “My name is”.
exercises.explanation: Use heiße with ich and heißt with du. Keep the capital letter at the beginning of a sentence.

exercises.prompt: Ask a peer “What is your name?” using the complete question taught here.
exercises.explanation: This is the name question from the lesson; recall it as a whole.

lessons.title: At the café
lessons.objective: Choose a drink and make a polite café request from memory.
lessons.explanation: Ich möchte means I would like. Learn einen Kaffee and einen Tee as complete request chunks: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. Kaffee and Tee are masculine nouns. Here they are the requested objects, so the article is einen. You will explore that pattern later; for now, swap the drink and keep einen. Bitte adds please; danke expresses thanks.

examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.
I would like a tea, please.

lessons.culturalNote: A greeting before a request and thanks afterward make this small exchange courteous.

exercises.prompt: You want tea. Which complete request matches your intention?
exercises.explanation: Change the drink while keeping the polite request frame.

exercises.prompt: Build the full polite request for one coffee.
exercises.explanation: Use einen in these requests, not ein. German nouns keep their capitals: Kaffee and Tee.

exercises.prompt: Read the café exchange. Which drink does the customer request?
exercises.explanation: The customer requests tea; the thanks closes the exchange.
exercises.passage:
Customer: Hallo. Einen Tee, bitte.
Server: Einen Tee?
Customer: Ja. Danke.
exercises.translation:
Customer: Hello. A tea, please.
Server: A tea?
Customer: Yes. Thank you.

exercises.prompt: Say “I would like a tea, please” using the full request frame.
exercises.explanation: Use einen in these requests, not ein. German nouns keep their capitals: Kaffee and Tee.

exercises.prompt: You arrive at a café and want coffee. Make the short request “A coffee, please”.
exercises.explanation: The short request still includes please.

exercises.prompt: Give the English meaning of this complete request: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.
answers: I would like a coffee, please.
exercises.explanation: This is a polite request, not a statement about having coffee.

lessons.title: Numbers and quantities
lessons.objective: Recognize one to ten, ask a price, and order a small quantity.
lessons.explanation: Count one through ten as two short runs. Then use Was kostet for a price and keep German noun capitals as you order a quantity.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

lessons.culturalNote: A price question can be brief and direct; bitte still makes a request polite.

exercises.prompt: Which German number means three?
exercises.explanation: Drei is three.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to ask the price of one coffee.
exercises.explanation: Was kostet asks what one thing costs.

exercises.prompt: Say in German: Two apples, please.
exercises.explanation: Äpfel is plural and remains capitalized.

exercises.prompt: Think: you want one coffee. Ask its price, then write the question.
exercises.explanation: The learned price question is Was kostet, followed by the item.
